```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(dataExplorer)
```

## Who is this for?

This app is for students exploring global development. It helps investigate:
**How does the relationship between income and life expectancy vary across
continents and years?**

The app uses the packaged `gapminder_data`: 142 countries observed at five-year
intervals from 1952 to 2007. No external data file or download is needed when
the app runs.

## Install and launch

Install from GitHub in an R session:

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes") # If needed
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-min-1303")
```

Then launch the app:

```{r launch, eval=FALSE}
library(dataExplorer)
launch_app(launch.browser = TRUE)
```

The interactive app runs until you stop it. Use RStudio's Stop button or Escape
in the console to return to R. When developing from the cloned project, run
`devtools::load_all()` before `launch_app()`.

## Understand the data

```{r data-fields}
head(gapminder_data, 3)
```

Each row represents a country in a year:

| Field | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `country` | Country name |
| `continent` | Continent grouping in the source dataset |
| `year` | Observation year |
| `lifeExp` | Life expectancy at birth, in years |
| `pop` | Total population |
| `gdpPercap` | GDP per capita, adjusted for purchasing power |

GDP per capita measures economic output per person, not a person's salary.
Population is included in the data but is not used to weight the app's medians
or the size of the plotted points.

## Follow an exploration

1. Start with all continents and **2007**. In the first plot, each country is a
   point. A point further right has higher GDP per capita; a point higher up
   has longer life expectancy. Colours and shapes identify continents. The
   income axis is logarithmic, so equal distances correspond to equal ratios.
2. Select only **Asia**. Look at the spread of its countries and the summary
   table. The table is calculated with `summarise_development()`.
3. Change the year to **1952**, then return to **2007**. Both axes stay fixed to
   make comparisons across selections easier. Check whether countries move
   into a different part of the income/life-expectancy space.
4. Look at the trend chart. It keeps the full time period and shows each selected
   continent's median country life expectancy. The dashed line follows the
   selected year. Add Europe or Africa to compare trajectories.

The app's table uses an exported function that can also be called directly:

```{r asia-summary}
asia_1952 <- summarise_development(1952, "Asia")
asia_2007 <- summarise_development(2007, "Asia")
comparison <- rbind(asia_1952, asia_2007)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 1)
```

For the `r asia_2007$countries` Asian countries represented, median country life
expectancy increased from `r round(asia_1952$median_life_exp, 1)` years in 1952 to
`r round(asia_2007$median_life_exp, 1)` years in 2007, a difference of
`r round(asia_2007$median_life_exp - asia_1952$median_life_exp, 1)` years.
Median GDP per capita also increased, from approximately
`r format(round(asia_1952$median_gdp_per_capita), big.mark = ",")` to
`r format(round(asia_2007$median_gdp_per_capita), big.mark = ",")` in the source
data's purchasing-power-adjusted units.

These summaries suggest that the typical country in this group had both higher
income and longer life expectancy by 2007. They do not describe every country,
and the two medians need not refer to the same country. Return to the scatter
plot to inspect the variation that these summaries conceal. This comparison
does not establish that higher income caused longer life expectancy.

## Try an empty or weak selection

Clear every checkbox under **Compare continents**. The app displays
"Select at least one continent to explore the data." rather than a misleading
empty chart or a technical error. Select Asia again to restore the outputs.

Select only **Oceania** to see another limitation: this dataset contains just
Australia and New Zealand for that continent. The app explains this beside the
snapshot, so the results should not be generalised to the whole region.

## Trace an input to an output

The app source is `inst/shiny/app.R`. Its year input has the identifier `year`.
Inside `server()`:

1. `selected_year()` converts `input$year` to a number and validates it against
   the available observation years.
2. `selected_continents()` validates `input$continents`, including the empty
   selection case.
3. `snapshot()` filters the packaged data using those two reactive values.
4. `output$comparison` uses `renderPlot()` to plot the filtered rows.

Changing a year invalidates the dependent reactive values and redraws the
snapshot. The separate `development_summary()` reactive calls the exported
`summarise_development()` function for each selected continent; its results feed
`output$summary`. The trend chart uses all years for the selected continents,
while its marker follows the chosen year.

## Limitations and attribution

These are historical country-level summaries, not estimates of present-day
conditions. Country medians weight each country equally rather than each
person equally. Country averages can hide inequalities within countries, and
continent summaries can hide substantial differences between countries.

The data are redistributed from Jennifer Bryan's
[gapminder R package](https://jennybc.github.io/gapminder/), version 1.0.1,
distributed under CC0, and originate from
[Gapminder](https://www.gapminder.org/data/).
The reproducible preparation script is `data-raw/gapminder_data.R`: it converts
`gapminder::gapminder` to a base data frame and saves the packaged dataset.
The repository README records the generative AI assistance used in this project.
